query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase, equiatomic high‐entropy alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi, reducing the grain size below a critical threshold promotes dynamic amorphization at the grain boundaries, which in turn increases lattice friction during dislocation activity. This mechanism governs the hardness and yield strength such that below a certain grain size the alloy shows an inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, equiatomic high‐entropy alloy (e.g. CoCrFeMnNi) exhibiting a conventional coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing to refine the grain size to an ultrafine regime (sub-micron) while maintaining a single-phase solid solution.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing (e.g. nanoindentation and uniaxial tensile or compression tests) performed at room temperature in an inert environment to preclude oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dynamically amorphized, ultra‐nanocrystalline layer at the grain boundaries during deformation.
generation.mechanism: With grain refinement, the increased fraction of grain boundaries becomes susceptible to stress‐induced amorphization. This amorphous (or near-amorphous) interfacial layer raises the dislocation nucleation barrier and leads to increased lattice friction, causing a non‐linear increase in hardness and yield strength (inverse Hall–Petch behavior) rather than a straightforward linear trend.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the coarse-grained baseline, the ultrafine-grained sample will exhibit higher hardness and yield strength. However, below a critical grain size, the strengthening effect will no longer scale linearly with grain size reduction due to the onset of dynamic amorphization at the boundaries.
generation.baseline: The coarse-grained high-entropy alloy demonstrating classical Hall–Petch behavior with predictable strength increases upon moderate grain refinement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloys processed in an inert (non-oxidizing) environment at room temperature. Its applicability to multiphase alloys or those with additional microstructural features (e.g., precipitates) remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical grain size where the transition from conventional to inverse Hall–Petch behavior occurs and the quantitative contribution of dynamic amorphization to the overall strength remain to be precisely determined and may depend on subtle compositional and processing variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples: one set with a coarse grain size (maintaining classical Hall–Petch behavior) and a second set with ultrafine grains achieved via severe plastic deformation or controlled thermomechanical processing. Perform in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) during mechanical loading on the ultrafine sample to observe the occurrence of grain-boundary amorphization. Carry out nanoindentation and uniaxial tensile/compression tests on both sets to quantitatively determine hardness and yield strength.
measurements: Grain size distribution (using EBSD or STEM)
In situ TEM observations of grain boundary structure during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not display an increase in hardness and yield strength over the coarse-grained samples, or if in situ TEM shows no evidence of stress‐induced amorphization at grain boundaries, then the hypothesis that dynamic grain-boundary amorphization governs the anomalous hardness/strength behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
